sections.h2: Quick ways to sell in North Hempstead
sections.html:
Owners here choose between a listing, a for-sale-by-owner sale and a direct cash purchase. The right pick depends on how much work the house needs and how soon you must close. First, settle which government covers your address, because this town of about 239,000 people contains 31 incorporated villages.

North Hempstead is one of three towns in Nassau County, on Long Island, with Manhasset as the town seat. The typical owner-occupied home is valued at $888,000, and 79.5% of housing is owner-occupied. Median gross rent is $2,318 a month and median household income is $158,158. At those values a sale puts real money at stake in repairs, carrying costs and tax proration, so compare a listing's net proceeds with a firm cash figure before you decide.

sections.h2: Town or village: who covers your house
sections.html:
When a house stands inside one of the 31 villages, the village sets its own zoning, and the town covers only the unincorporated hamlets. The town's Department of Building, Safety, Inspection and Enforcement administers State and Town codes in those unincorporated areas.

Villages include Great Neck, Roslyn, Westbury, Mineola, Williston Park, Lake Success, Sands Point and Kings Point. Town-governed hamlets include Manhasset, Port Washington, Roslyn Heights, Carle Place, New Cassel, Albertson, Herricks and Searingtown. Check your tax bill or ask the town which applies before you request permit records, because a village house needs the village hall.

For hamlet properties, the town's Inspection Section issues building, plumbing and rental permits, and the Enforcement Section investigates construction and illegal housing complaints. Permit applications and records go through the town's online portal, and the building department's number is (516) 869-6311. An open permit or an illegal conversion is the kind of problem that stalls a conventional sale, so look for them early.

No new village has formed in the town since Port Washington North in May 1932, so the patchwork is permanent: two houses a block apart can answer to different building departments.

North Hempstead has two tax levies with different years, so the split at closing depends on the closing date. The Receiver of Taxes publishes a closing guide for attorneys and title companies that explains the periods.

Levy periods in North Hempstead
LevyPeriod covered
School, first halfJuly 1 to December 31
School, second halfJanuary 1 to June 30
General, first halfJanuary 1 to June 30
General, second halfJuly 1 to December 31

School levies follow a July to June year, while general levies follow the calendar year. Incorporated villages bill their own taxes and may use assessed values that differ from the county roll, so a village owner has a third bill to settle. The Nassau County Department of Assessment manages assessments, and improvements made before a sale, including unreported work, can lift the assessed value beyond the 6% cap.

Two details catch sellers by surprise. Exemptions generally do not pass to the buyer, so a buyer must apply for their own. Nassau County can also add prorated restored taxes to a future bill when an exemption is removed after a sale, and that can take up to two years to appear.

The town splits across many districts, so the district code on your bill is the fact to check. The Receiver of Taxes lists codes for districts including Westbury, Roslyn, Port Washington, Manhasset, Great Neck, Herricks, Mineola, Carle Place and Jericho. Residency disputes go to the school district or the State Education Department, not to the town.

The seller pays New York's base transfer tax of $2 for each $500 of price on a conveyance outside New York City, and the TP-584 return is filed with the county clerk where the property sits. For North Hempstead that is the Nassau County Clerk, at (516) 571-2664.

The state also applies an additional one percent buyer-paid tax on residences priced at $1 million or more. With a median owner-occupied value of $888,000, sales near that line are a live question for sellers and their buyers. The TP-584 and any tax are due no later than the 15th day after the deed is delivered.

If an LLC owns the house or will buy it, tell your attorney early. The state requires names and addresses of members, managers and other authorized persons when an LLC is on either side of a transfer of a building with up to four dwelling units.

Most of the town's growth landed between 1930 and 1960, so many houses are decades old and have had additions. Check the year built on your tax record and gather permit paperwork for later work before you list or take an offer. Weather also takes a toll, with about 45 inches of precipitation and 23 inches of snow a year in Manhasset, so roofs and basements deserve a look.

sections.h2: What to do before you accept an offer
sections.html:
Work through a short checklist. Confirm whether the town or a village covers your house. Pull the permit record, since open permits and illegal conversions are what stall mortgage buyers. Request tax proration figures from the Receiver of Taxes using the closing guide. Tell your attorney about any LLC involved. Then compare offers on what you actually net: a listing may bring a higher price but adds repairs and time, while a direct cash sale can close on a date you choose and takes the house as it stands.

On closing day your attorney handles the TP-584 filing with the Nassau County Clerk, and the deed is recorded afterward. If you had STAR, remember that your buyer applies for their own exemptions; yours does not transfer.

faqs.q: Does the town or the village issue permits for my North Hempstead house?
faqs.a: That depends on the address. The town covers unincorporated hamlets such as Manhasset and Port Washington, and each of the 31 incorporated villages handles its own zoning. Check your tax bill or call the town if you are unsure.

faqs.q: Which office collects the tax bill for a North Hempstead house?
faqs.a: The Town Receiver of Taxes collects the town's general and school taxes, and incorporated villages collect their own village taxes. Nassau County's Department of Assessment sets the assessment.

faqs.q: Do exemptions like STAR carry over to the buyer?
faqs.a: Generally no. The buyer applies for their own exemptions through the Nassau County Department of Assessment, and a buyer who purchased after January 2, 2015 may be eligible for the STAR Credit program.

faqs.q: Who records the deed in North Hempstead?
faqs.a: The Nassau County Clerk records it. The seller pays the state transfer tax of $2 per $500, and the TP-584 is due within 15 days of the deed delivery.

faqs.q: How do I find my school district code?
faqs.a: Look it up on your tax bill or in the County Assessor's property search. The town lists codes from 001 for Westbury to 315 for Jericho, and residency disputes go to the district.
